system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 8 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2173-05-03 14:27:00 to 2173-05-10 14:50:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a 58-year-old male with a history of acute myeloid leukemia in remission, chronic systolic heart failure (LVEF 25%), and chronic kidney disease, was admitted for acute nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and fever following potential exposure to family with gastroenteritis. He presented with dehydration, hypotension, and acute kidney injury with metabolic acidosis. Initial management included IV fluid resuscitation and empiric antibiotics. His course was complicated by pulmonary edema on hospital day 3, requiring IV furosemide. Diarrhea improved with loperamide, psyllium, and cholestyramine. Stool testing later confirmed rotavirus. Renal function improved with hydration, and he was discharged euvolemic, off oxygen, with instructions to restart furosemide when diarrhea resolved and to follow up with nephrology for ongoing kidney disease management.
problems: Acute on chronic systolic heart failure
Acute kidney failure with lesion of tubular necrosis

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, I'm Dr. Patel. I've been reviewing your case. You came in today because of worsening shortness of breath and two episodes of near fainting at home. Can you tell me more about how you've been feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. I’ve been struggling to catch my breath, especially when I walk or even just stand up. I felt dizzy twice last night—like I was going to pass out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And were you using more oxygen at home than usual?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve needed it even just to talk or eat. My wife said I sounded like I was wheezing at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ve done some tests. Your chest X-ray shows no pneumonia, but your CT scan shows fluid buildup in your lungs and around them—what we call pleural effusions. This is likely due to your heart not pumping well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My heart again? I thought I was doing okay with my medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your heart function is still reduced. Your ejection fraction is now about 20%, which is lower than before. That means your heart isn’t pumping as efficiently, and fluid is backing up into your lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s why I can’t breathe well. Is it because I stopped my Lasix?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You mentioned you stopped your furosemide because of diarrhea last month. That likely contributed to the fluid buildup. We’re restarting it now through IV to help you breathe better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need to stay on it forever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s part of your long-term plan. But we have to balance it with your kidney function, which has been affected too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My kidneys… they’ve been bad for a while. My last creatinine was 3.0, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and it’s now up to 3.9. The diuretics can stress your kidneys, so we’ll monitor closely and adjust as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about dialysis. My family wants to wait until after our trips.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But your nephrologist recommends starting soon. Fluid overload like this can keep making your breathing worse. We’ve scheduled your fistula placement and moved up your appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… I guess we need to face it sooner rather than later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll support you through it. Now, your blood work also shows metabolic acidosis, but it’s improving with treatment and not severe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from my kidneys too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your kidneys help balance your body’s acid levels. When they’re not working well, acid can build up. But your lactate is normal, so it’s not from poor oxygen delivery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. What about my lungs? I’ve had BOOP for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The pulmonologist reviewed your CT. There’s no sign of worsening BOOP or infection. The V/Q scan was normal, so no pulmonary embolism. Your breathing issues are mostly from fluid, not your lungs flaring up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I don’t need more steroids?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. We’ll keep you on your current 2 mg of prednisone for GVHD. Increasing it could affect your blood sugar and bones.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I’ve been on that for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Johnson. Your labs are improving. Your creatinine is coming down, and your breathing is better. We’ve switched you from IV to oral furosemide.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I feel less puffed out. Can I walk a bit more today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll get physical therapy to help. You’re deconditioned, and we want to build your strength before you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been so tired lately. Is that from the heart or the steroids?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely both. Your heart isn’t pumping efficiently, and long-term steroid use can cause muscle weakness. We’ll monitor and adjust as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about that heart MRI I had yesterday?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The results just came in. Your heart is enlarged, and the ejection fraction is 18%, which confirms severe systolic dysfunction. But there’s no sign of inflammation or iron overload.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So is it from the chemo or GVHD?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The cardiologist thinks it’s likely from prior chemotherapy. No signs of active cardiac GVHD, so we won’t change your steroids for that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad it’s not getting worse. Will I keep the same heart meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue metoprolol and aspirin. Your outpatient cardiologist will follow up early next month.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your kidney function is stabilizing. Creatinine is back to 3.2. We’re keeping you on your home dose of Lasix.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Any word from nephrology?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your fistula placement is scheduled. They emphasized starting dialysis soon to prevent another hospitalization like this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll talk to my wife. We’ll rearrange our plans.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Your oxygen levels are stable, and you’re walking with less shortness of breath. We’re planning for discharge in a couple of days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Will I still need oxygen at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just for activity and coughing spells—same as before. Your baseline hasn’t changed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my diarrhea? I’ve been using loperamide.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s improved. Continue cholestyramine and psyllium as needed. No signs of infection—your stool cultures were negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check: your labs are stable, you’re breathing well, and your heart and kidney function are as good as we can get them for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, you’re cleared for discharge tomorrow morning. Let’s go over your medications and follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nephrology in two weeks for dialysis planning. Cardiology follow-up early next month. Pulmonology says your BOOP is stable—no changes needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I start feeling short of breath again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor or come back. Don’t stop your Lasix unless instructed. Watch for swelling or weight gain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, your discharge orders are ready. You’re going home with your regular medications and oxygen as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Stay on your renal diet, take your phosphate binders, and monitor your symptoms. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a 58-year-old male with a history of acute myeloid leukemia in remission, post-transplant graft-versus-host disease, systolic heart failure, and chronic kidney disease, was admitted for worsening shortness of breath and near syncope at home. He was found to have acute on chronic heart failure with pulmonary edema and bilateral pleural effusions, leading to hypoxic respiratory failure. Treatment with intravenous furosemide improved his symptoms, though his renal function temporarily worsened, requiring careful management. His metabolic acidosis resolved, and imaging ruled out pulmonary embolism or infection. A non-contrast cardiac MRI showed severe left ventricular dysfunction without evidence of myocardial inflammation or iron overload. He was stabilized on home diuretics, with plans to initiate outpatient dialysis and follow-up with nephrology, cardiology, and pulmonology. He was discharged home with improved oxygenation and stable vital signs, continuing all baseline medications.
